items.summary: Google DeepMind has announced Genie 4, a new version of its world model. A world model is an AI system that can simulate a virtual environment. The company says Genie 4 offers a big jump in realism and works in real time, meaning the simulated world responds as you use it. The source text is brief and gives no further details, such as how the model works, how it was tested, or when people can try it.

items.headline: Dementia Research Group Uses NVIDIA AI to Tap Hidden Data
items.summary: About 57 million people live with dementia, and no treatment yet stops or reverses Alzheimer's. Researchers face too much data, too few experts to review it, and slow progress. A group called C-BRAIN, led by Dr. Randall Bateman and made up of 18 institutions, launched in November 2025 to speed things up with AI. It is working with NVIDIA. The group wants to use "dark data," such as unpublished results and private data that AI tools have never seen. To protect privacy, AI models learn from data at each institution without the data leaving it. C-BRAIN runs 64 NVIDIA GPUs, which are powerful computer chips, plus cloud systems on Microsoft Azure. It has built two tools so far, OpenScientist and InsightEngine.

items.headline: Retell credits OpenAI models for powering 100M monthly voice calls
items.summary: Retell, a company that builds voice agents, uses OpenAI models to help handle about 100 million calls each month. Voice agents are AI programs that talk with people on the phone. According to OpenAI's blog, a model called GPT-6 Astra ranks first on Retell's own benchmark, which is a test used to compare how well voice agents perform. The post also says Retell uses Codex, OpenAI's coding tool, and that this helps the company reach an annual revenue run rate of $1.6 million per employee. A run rate projects yearly income from current earnings. The source gives few other details, but it shows how a small team can use AI tools to serve a very large number of customers.

items.headline: Manufacturers urged to turn factory know-how into shared 'industrial intelligence'
items.summary: MIT Technology Review looks at how manufacturers can get more value from what they already know. It calls this 'industrial intelligence': a firm's know-how, work practices, production data and understanding of its business. Much of it sits with experienced workers or in single plants. The piece says connecting it can help more teams use it. It also describes 'physical AI', meaning systems that sense conditions, reason about them and act in the real world. One example is a robot adjusting to varied parts within safe limits. Toyota Industries linked paint shop data and reports analysis time fell from five days to under four hours. Its pilot cut related paint defects by about 25%. The article says data shows what is happening, while industrial intelligence adds context for what should happen and when people must step in.

items.headline: OpenAI and Oracle expand partnership to bring Oracle apps into ChatGPT
items.summary: OpenAI and Oracle are growing their partnership. The goal is to bring Oracle's business applications and AI agents into ChatGPT. An AI agent is a program that can carry out tasks for a user instead of only answering questions. The deal will also help power new Oracle products. For companies that use Oracle software, this could mean working with those tools directly inside ChatGPT. The announcement gives few other details.

items.headline: Check Point uses OpenAI Daybreak to speed up vulnerability research
items.summary: Security company Check Point is using OpenAI Daybreak to move faster on the research behind its new protections. According to OpenAI's blog, the tool helps Check Point's analysts turn vulnerability intelligence, which is information about weaknesses in software, into defenses for customers more quickly. The post gives few other details here. It matters because the faster a security firm can act on a known weakness, the sooner its customers can be protected.

items.headline: TAO Scheduler Speeds Up AI Agents by Planning Around Tool Delays
items.summary: AI agents often switch between two jobs. The AI model thinks on a cluster of GPUs, then waits for outside tools running on regular computer chips. Researchers say current systems ignore whether a tool has finished, so scarce GPU space gets wasted. They also use rough rules to decide which waiting sessions to run and where. The team built TAO, a scheduler that looks at how soon a tool will return, what saved data a GPU already holds, and how many tokens (small chunks of text) a session uses. It then picks and places sessions together using a planning method called dynamic programming. Across 12 tested setups, TAO cut latency by up to 26.8% and time to first token by up to 36.3%. It raised decode throughput by up to 29.5%. These gains are measured against the best existing baseline for each metric.

items.headline: New Quaternion-Based Networks Spot Rotated Objects With Fewer Parameters
items.summary: Researchers introduced Quaternion Approximate Networks, or QUAN, a new way to build image-recognition models that handle rotation well. Quaternions are a type of math used to describe 3D rotation. Earlier quaternion networks tried to work fully in that math. QUAN instead approximates it using ordinary real-number operations, which keeps the geometry while running efficiently on custom GPU code. The team also added a training-stability method called Independent Quaternion Batch Normalization and applied quaternion ideas to attention. Tests covered image classification, object detection and robotic perception. QUAN reached higher accuracy with fewer parameters and faster training than standard and quaternion models. In detection, it was more parameter-efficient and handled rotation better than standard CNNs. The authors say it could suit robots with limited computing power.

items.headline: EmbeddingGemma 2 Maps Text, Images, Audio and Video Into One Space
items.summary: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a new open model that turns text, images, audio, video, and mixes of them into numbers called embeddings. These numbers let computers compare and search different kinds of content in one shared space. The team used simpler per-layer embeddings and trained the model in stages, adding new content types and goals step by step. The authors say it sets a new best balance of quality and size across benchmarks for all content types. They report it beats specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. It also suits limited hardware: users can load only the parts they need, limit image detail, shorten the embeddings, or use compressed weights. The model is released to support further research.

items.headline: New Training Method Teaches AI to Link Visual Clues Across an Image
items.summary: Researchers built EvidenceConnect, a way to create training data for vision-language models, which are AI systems that read both images and text. The data comes from zoomed-in views of related parts of one image. Questions made from them require comparing, combining, or chaining visual clues. To keep quality high, an answer is kept only if several independent models agree on it. Questions are also dropped if the answer still holds after key regions are removed. The team trained models with RLVR, a method that rewards correct answers, and called the result ZwZ2. It improved fine detail and spatial perception. It also helped with embodied spatial reasoning, long multimodal inputs, agent tasks, and general visual reasoning, even though the data was not built for those tests. The authors say strengthening this shared skill of connecting evidence makes AI perception more general.

items.headline: Discrete image tokens can now match continuous ones at understanding pictures
items.summary: AI models can turn images into discrete tokens, like words in a language. This lets one model handle text and images the same way. Many researchers thought this process always loses meaning, so continuous image representations would stay better. This paper questions that idea. The authors find that rounding error is not a good predictor of quality. What matters more is how many bits the token codes carry. Existing methods stop improving as more codebooks are added. The team proposes Factorized Vector Quantization, which splits an image feature into several views and encodes each with its own codebook. It keeps improving with more bits and matches continuous representations on understanding tasks. It beats UniAR by 22.8% and Emu3-Chat by 59.2% on a nine-metric average. It is also the first discrete model competitive with Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained text reading. Code and models are public.

items.headline: Study finds common memory shortcuts fail when AI groups make decisions
items.summary: When several AI agents discuss a problem, their talk is often squeezed into short notes for a final decision maker. This paper asks what those notes should keep. Researchers built CrossProfile, a test of 480 tasks, and tried models including Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B and two DeepSeek models. Keeping only the rarest facts did no better than picking at random. Keeping only facts on topic let in decoys, which are misleading facts that sound relevant. Accuracy depended on the mix of evidence kept, not on the method used. The decision model also trusted facts said by many agents. Removing the agent name tags raised accuracy by 13 to 24 points in the classic setup. In natural discussions, the full transcript did worse than no notes at all.

items.headline: New benchmark tests AI agents that make videos by writing code
items.summary: Researchers released VibeVideoBench, a test for AI agents that build videos by writing code instead of using video-generating models. Regular video models struggle with exact formulas, correct charts and narration that matches the screen. The benchmark has 239 tasks in English and Chinese, such as data stories, classroom lessons and paper explainers. Each agent has one hour to deliver a finished MP4 with sound. Nine top agent systems were tested. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 ranked first and second, agreeing with human reviewers. The best system met every core requirement on 76.3% of tasks. Many failures were not about quality. About three quarters of lost videos came from final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never began. This shows agents still plan their time poorly.

items.headline: RynnWorld-Latent Teaches One Video Model to Predict Actions Across Many Robots
items.summary: Robots use different control systems, and human videos come with no control labels. That makes it hard to train one model on all of them. RynnWorld-Latent tackles this with "latent actions," a shared way to describe movement that works for any body. The model was pretrained on 23 datasets, about 553.5 million video frames, drawn from human videos, robot demos and simulations. It can also create synthetic training demos in two ways. Tests showed better video prediction, and the model followed different action sequences from the same starting scene. Training with its synthetic data raised policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and on real robots. The authors say this shared action format could help models learn how the physical world responds across many kinds of robots.

items.headline: PDRVLA Teaches Robot Models Physics Without Slow Video Generation
items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models turn camera images and written instructions into robot actions. But they often understand physics poorly. Video world models grasp how scenes change, yet making future videos slows a robot's control loop. PDRVLA takes a lighter route. A small Physical Dynamics Module pulls out physical tokens, which are compact summaries of how a scene may change, and uses them to guide actions. It learns by predicting future color images, depth, and motion features, with extra guidance from a frozen video world model. It needs no video generation while running. Training uses only public data, expanded with human-to-robot synthesis and extra annotations. In four simulation tests, it scored 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv.

items.headline: Study: AI Agents Learn Their Harness, Not Just the Task
items.summary: AI agents run inside a harness, meaning the prompts, tools, and control rules that present a task to the model. Researchers show that a trained agent absorbs the preferences of the harness it was trained in. They split an agent's results into two parts: the harness's ceiling, or best possible return, minus the agent's mismatch, or return lost to poor decisions. Testing an agent with a fixed model mixes these two parts together. In a web-task benchmark, just reversing the order of the observation fields cut a trained model's success from 85.0% to 19.2%, though the best choices stayed the same. Harnesses that looked worse in fixed-model tests but had a higher ceiling beat the original after more training. The authors have released their code.

items.headline: Teach AI what to draw first, then how to draw it
items.summary: Researchers propose a two-step way to train image generators. First, a model learns what things are and mean by predicting image pieces one after another, called autoregressive pretraining. Then a diffusion model, which cleans up noise into sharp pictures, handles the fine pixel details. Tests showed the first step helps the second learn faster and produce better images. They also found that meaning matters more than how good the first-stage images look. So they built a tokenizer, a tool that turns images into pieces, trained only with text guidance. Using scaling laws to plan compute, they trained a 3-billion-parameter text-to-image model in just 6,600 H100 GPU-hours. It scored 86 on GenEval and 87 on DPG-Bench.

items.headline: OpenAI Releases GPT-6.1 Terra, a Faster Midrange Model
items.summary: OpenAI has launched GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast and efficient model. It focuses on visual reasoning, computer use and clearer writing. OpenAI says it suits workday tasks like drafting proposals, reading technical drawings, filling out forms and editing videos. Blogger Simon Willison notes Terra sits in the middle of the lineup, much like Sonnet in Anthropic's models. OpenAI's Ted Sanders says it beats Astra and Sol at technical writing and matches them on vision and computer use, but runs much faster. It is a bit worse on most other things. Terra costs $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens. That is almost half the price of Sol, and around 10 times the price of the smaller Luna model.

items.headline: Greptile uses OpenAI tools to catch bugs beyond code review
items.summary: Greptile, a company that finds bugs in software code, is using several OpenAI tools to go further than standard code review. According to OpenAI's blog, Greptile uses GPT-6 Astra to test how users move through a product, which are known as user workflows. It uses Daybreak to strengthen security. It also uses Codex to reduce rework, meaning less time spent fixing the same problems twice. The source gives only a short description, so details on results or how each tool works are not provided.

items.headline: ChatGPT Keeps Sending Tech Support Questions to 404 Media
items.summary: Jason Koebler of 404 Media says many people now ask ChatGPT for help with everyday tech problems. They do this because big tech platforms offer almost no customer support and make it hard to reach a human. He writes that ChatGPT is increasingly telling these users they have found something worth reporting. It also tells them that 404 Media can help. But these are normal tech support problems, not news stories. The quote shows how AI chatbots can send people to the wrong place, and how a lack of real customer support pushes people toward them.

items.headline: Anthropic's IPO filing warns its own AI could pose existential risks
items.summary: Anthropic has filed a 335-page prospectus for its stock market debut. About 100 pages cover risks. The company says its technology could harm society, upset global politics and, if things go wrong, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. It asks buyers to see the stock as a chance to be part of something bigger. The article argues Anthropic is skilled at telling a dramatic story. Cofounder Jack Clark told an IMF meeting that the singularity, the point where tech outpaces its makers, has already begun. Cofounder Chris Olah told the Vatican the company finds unsettling signs in its models. The filing even lists questions about whether its AI has feelings as a business risk. The author says the company may be right, but notes many researchers doubt such claims.

items.headline: Webframe runs web pages like programs, and Simon Willison tests it
items.summary: Webframe is a small project by Jeff Lindsay. You point it at a web address or file, and it runs the page in a hidden browser window. Anything the page logs goes to standard output, and any errors go to standard error. It is written in Go and uses the system's own browser engine on Mac, Linux and Windows, so it does not carry its own browser. Simon Willison says it resembles his shot-scraper tool, but in a smaller package that does not need Playwright, a browser automation tool. He asked Claude Opus 5.5 to try it out, build a few prototypes, and write a report on how well it works as a web scraper and as a sandbox, meaning a safe space to run code.

items.headline: Google Adds Brain Science Lesson to Its AI Quests Series
items.summary: Google has released a new lesson in its AI Quests series. It is called "Polar Peaks" and focuses on neuroscience, the study of the brain and nervous system. The series is meant to teach AI literacy, which means understanding the basics of what AI is and how it works. The new lesson ties that learning to the topic of mapping the human brain. The source gives few other details, such as the age group or how long the lesson takes. Still, it shows Google using real science topics to help people learn about AI.

items.headline: Op-ed: AI Safety Focus Misses Everyday Harms to Young People
items.summary: An opinion piece in MIT Technology Review argues that tech policy looks only at the worst-case harms of a product. Examples include a chatbot promising not to encourage suicide, or a platform limiting teen access to fentanyl. The author says these steps matter but set a low bar. Products can pass them and still leave young people hooked on AI companions or endless feeds. The piece says companies like these narrow goals because they cut lawsuits and ease pressure for tougher rules. It says Google backed state chatbot bills with broad exemptions, while stronger bills on emotional dependence failed. The author urges policymakers to protect how people think, learn and connect, not only to prevent disasters.

items.headline: AI Search weekly roundup covers new models, voice tools and AI cybersecurity
items.summary: AI Search, a YouTube channel, posted its latest AI news roundup. It covers dozens of items in about 40 minutes. Models and tools named include Kimi K3.1 Pro, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Fibo 2.0, Hi3D 1.0, Dessa, Claude Duet and Ideogram Vector. The video also has sections on AI cybersecurity, OpenAI research agents for complex biological data, and a humanoid robot called Unitree H2X. Luma sponsors the video. The description only lists topics and links, so it gives no details on what each tool can do. Viewers would need to open the video or the linked pages to learn more.

items.headline: AI Search Reviews New Deepseek V4.1 Flash Model and DeepInfer Tool
items.summary: The YouTube channel AI Search has posted a review of a new model from Deepseek, called Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017. The video also covers DeepInfer, a separate project from Deepseek that is shared on GitHub. The model is listed on Hugging Face, a site where AI models are shared. The reviewer tries it on many tasks, including a math explainer, building an Unreal game, composing music, a Blender VR scene, identifying cancer, deep research and idea generation. The video also goes over the model's specs and benchmarks, which are scores from standard tests. The description gives no results, so how well the model performs is not stated here.

items.headline: Kazakhstan Builds Up AI Computing as Nvidia's Jensen Huang Visits Astana
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana on Oct. 23. He met President Tokayev and joined a public talk with Kazakhstan's AI minister, Zhaslan Madiyev. Madiyev said the country wants AI that speaks Kazakh and understands its culture. Huang said Kazakhstan could turn its energy into intelligence and export it. He also said a country's data is its natural resource. Nvidia announced an investment in Higgsfield AI, a startup founded in Kazakhstan. On infrastructure, a company called Firebird signed an investment deal with the government. It has a U.S. export license for 45,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips. The first phase is being built with Kazakhtelecom, aiming to launch commercially in the third quarter of 2027.

items.headline: Hugging Face Blog Asks If Your Model Runs on AWS Trainium
items.summary: Hugging Face has published a blog post titled "Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up." The title suggests a way to check whether a given AI model works on Trainium, a chip made by Amazon Web Services for training AI models. The full text was not available, so details about how the lookup works are unknown. Still, the topic matters for developers who want to know if their models can run on this hardware before they commit to it.

items.headline: Hugging Face Blog Post Covers Training AI Agents With Database Grading Rewards
items.summary: Hugging Face published a blog post titled "Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox." The full text was not available, so details are limited. The title suggests the post is about reinforcement learning, or RL, a way of training AI by giving it scores for its actions. It also points to using grades stored in a database as those scores, and to training agents after their main training is done. ThinkingBox appears to be the tool or method involved. The exact approach and results are not known from the title alone.

items.headline: Why the system around an AI model matters more than the model
items.summary: An MIT Technology Review piece argues that the edge in enterprise AI now comes less from picking a model and more from the "serving harness," the engineering system around it. This covers architecture, memory use, and scheduling. The article says teams should start with the workload, since a fast customer chat tool needs differ from an overnight document job. A slightly better model may not be worth it if it doubles costs or misses speed targets. It also warns that these choices affect one another. For example, GPU memory can run short as more users connect, even when computing power is free. Its advice: measure first, find the main bottleneck, fix it, then measure again.

items.headline: Vanguard AI Leader Explains How to Build Scalable AI in Finance
items.summary: MIT Technology Review shared a session from its EmTech Future conference on building AI that can grow safely. The speaker is Jing Wang, who leads Vanguard's Center for AI and Insights. The talk says a strong base needs data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance (the rules and oversight) working as one. It looks at how to do this in a highly regulated setting like finance. It also covers how responsible, trustworthy use can turn new tools, including agentic systems (AI that can take actions on its own), into lasting value for investors.

items.headline: Microsoft Research unveils Flint-interactive for building interactive AI-made charts
items.summary: Microsoft Research has released Flint-interactive, a language for making interactive data charts. It is built on top of Flint, an existing tool. AI agents can already make charts, but static ones limit exploring. Users want to click, filter, zoom and highlight across charts and text. Doing this with AI is costly and often breaks, since agents need many rounds of coding and debugging. Flint-interactive lets users or agents describe interactions in simple, high-level terms. Flint's compiler, the program that translates instructions, turns clicks and selections into events that carry meaning, then updates the visuals. This handles tricky layout and dependency problems. It could make dashboards and data stories easier and more reliable to build.

items.headline: NVIDIA launches Minerva to spot problems in giant AI data centers
items.summary: NVIDIA has launched Minerva, a software platform that helps teams watch over AI factories, the huge data centers that train and run AI models. At this scale, one weak part, like an overheated GPU, can slow a whole job. Minerva gathers data from chips, networks, storage and running jobs. It builds a map of how everything connects and uses AI to spot odd behavior, predict failures and group many alerts into one issue with a likely cause. It also has a chat assistant that suggests fixes. IREN says it helps its team do more planned maintenance. Aolani, Bitdeer AI, IBM, Jio, Lambda, Quake AI and Tesla plan to use it. Dell, Lenovo and Supermicro will offer it.

items.headline: DeepMind Maps Forest Types Across the Whole World
items.summary: Google DeepMind has published a global map that sorts forests into different types. It covers every 10-meter patch of land on Earth, roughly the size of a small room. This goes beyond simply showing where trees are. Knowing what kind of forest grows in a place gives a fuller picture of the land. The source gives few other details, such as how the map was built or how accurate it is.

items.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Launches on GeForce NOW Cloud Gaming
items.summary: NVIDIA says Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is available on its GeForce NOW cloud gaming service at launch. Players can stream the new campaign, multiplayer and the DMZ extraction mode without downloading the game. Ultimate members get GeForce RTX 5080-class power in the cloud, which lets the campaign use ray tracing, a method for more realistic light and shadows. NVIDIA also says existing Fire TV Stick users can now buy one-month Performance or Ultimate memberships directly through Amazon. Square Enix's FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE also joins the service this week, as part of six new games. The updates make it easier to play big games on devices without a powerful PC.

items.headline: Why business AI needs context to make good decisions
items.summary: MIT Technology Review's Business Lab, made with Celonis, looks at why company AI often falls short. Devavrat Shah, Celonis's chief scientist of enterprise AI, says AI agents need to know how a business really works. Without that, they can miss limits, make costly mistakes, or waste computing power. He suggests adding a layer of business context, set guardrails, and human review of recommendations. Companies should start with one specific decision, find its hardest steps, and test whether AI helps. Gains in speed and value can show if it is worth scaling. Shah says this could free staff for more strategic work, but companies must train employees to understand AI outputs instead of simply handing over decisions.

items.headline: AI's hidden cost: the storage left behind by every prompt
items.summary: When people think about AI costs, they picture GPUs, the chips that power models. But data storage is a growing expense that often gets missed. Every time a model answers a request, it leaves data behind, such as logs, cached context, backups and safety records. Western Digital (WD) measured one 8-second AI video. The user got a 3.97MB file, but more than 500MB of data stayed on the back end. That is about 130 times larger. McKinsey expects inference demand to grow 35% a year through 2030, faster than training at 22%. A WD-sponsored IDC survey of 763 decision makers found nearly 95% saw data volumes rise because of generative AI. The article argues that budgets focused only on compute may be too narrow, since slow data access can leave costly GPUs idle.

items.headline: Hugging Face Blog Looks at Ensemble Forecasting With IBM Granite Models
items.summary: Hugging Face has published a blog post titled "Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models." Based on the title, it covers how to combine several forecasting models, known as an ensemble, using IBM's Granite models built for time-series data. Time-series data is information recorded over time, such as sales or weather readings. The full text was not available, so details about the method, results, or tools are not known. The title suggests the post is a guide to using IBM's models together for forecasting.

items.headline: European banks use open AI models on their own infrastructure, NVIDIA says
items.summary: At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA showed how European banks and finance firms are building their own AI with open weight models, which are models whose settings anyone can download and adapt. Revolut is moving to one foundation model, PRAGMA, serving 80 million customers. Lloyds built ATUM to learn from billions of transactions. Bunq says its assistant Finn matches leading closed models at 60% of the cost per answer. Stripe reports 42x faster data pipelines in offline tests for its fraud detection. The pitch is that banks can keep control of their data and costs.

items.headline: NVIDIA Expands Cosmos With New Tools for Building World Models
items.summary: NVIDIA has added new training tools, simulation checkpoints and data blueprints to its Cosmos platform. Cosmos helps developers build world models, which are AI systems that understand and simulate the real world for robots and self-driving cars. The Cosmos Data Factory now offers five cloud blueprints for tasks like making synthetic driving scenes, defect images and weather changes in video. Porsche expects to cut repeated test drives by up to 90% using it. ANYbotics made over 1,500 synthetic clips to train inspection robots. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA also extended Cosmos Framework tools to more open models, including GR00T, Alpamayo, QWEN and Pi0.5. Developers can fine-tune, shrink and deploy them faster.

items.headline: Energy firms adopt NVIDIA DSX to tackle AI's power bottleneck
items.summary: Power is now the biggest bottleneck for building AI infrastructure. NVIDIA says over $300 billion in equipment is backlogged, and more than 200 gigawatts of projects wait in U.S. grid connection queues. NVIDIA's DSX platform tries to fix this by treating the power grid and the AI factory as one system. Engineers can simulate both before building, and AI factories can adjust their demand to grid conditions. GE Vernova, Hitachi Energy, Schneider Electric and Siemens Energy are building on it. Phaidra says its tools give about 10% more compute in the same power limit. Emerald AI says its approach could unlock up to 100 gigawatts on the existing U.S. grid.

items.headline: 31-Year-Old KLS Conjecture in Geometry Solved With Human-Directed AI Help
items.summary: Researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang of Microsoft Research, say they have proved the KLS conjecture, a math problem posed in 1995. It asks whether a simple flat cut is nearly as good as any curved cut at splitting a high-dimensional shape or probability distribution at its narrowest point. The proof shows the gap stays within a fixed constant, no matter how many dimensions there are. This matters because the cuts affect how fast random walks can explore a distribution, which underpins sampling methods used in statistics, optimization and computer science. The team worked with AI agents in a process directed by humans. The AI explored more than 100 possible approaches, while the researchers judged, trimmed and redirected the search. Other researchers have checked the work, and a machine-checked formal verification followed.

items.headline: AI Adoption Pushes Southeast Asia's Digital Economy Toward $368 Billion
items.summary: A Google AI blog post says Southeast Asia's digital economy is growing fast, and AI is a main reason. The region's digital economy is projected to reach $368 billion in 2026. It is expected to climb to $1 trillion by 2035. The post credits widespread use of AI for this growth. The digital economy means money made from online activity, such as e-commerce, digital services and online platforms. The source gives few other details, but the figures suggest AI could play a large role in the region's economic future.

items.headline: Microsoft podcast: researcher Chris White on tech built for real-world good
items.summary: In a Microsoft Research Podcast episode, program manager Weishung Liu talks with Chris White, who leads Microsoft Research's Catalyst Lab. White began as a postdoc at DARPA, the US defense research agency. In 2010 he worked on whether a new way of analyzing data could protect troops in Afghanistan. DARPA then asked him to prove its value on the ground, so he left academic research to help lead advanced tech work there. Later, he helped build dark-web search tools used to fight human trafficking. He won a 2016 Presidential Award for this work. The talk covers how he picks problems to solve and how he stays hopeful after seeing the worst of human behavior.

items.headline: Video Walks Through MOSS Image, a New Local AI Image Maker
items.summary: A new video from AI Search looks at MOSS Image, an AI image generator that can run on your own computer. The host calls it the new top local option. The video covers its specs, demos, and a comparison with Krea 2. It then shows how to set it up in ComfyUI, a popular tool for running image models. Other parts explain layout control, adding LoRAs (small add-on files that change a model's style), and ways to make it run faster. It also shows how to edit images and train your own LoRAs. Links to the model files are listed in the description. The video is sponsored by Higgsfield.

items.headline: Two Minute Papers Looks at Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 Argon
items.summary: A new Two Minute Papers video covers Gemini 4 Argon, an AI model from Google DeepMind. The title says the model is not what the host expected. The video description does not explain what the model can do or how it performs. It does link to the official model card, which is a short document describing an AI model, and to a safety report from DeepMind. It also points to social media posts from users and a benchmark site called Star Skirmish. These links suggest the video draws on early user reactions and test results. Anyone who wants details should read the model card and safety report directly.

tldr.intro: Today's stories focus on AI security and tooling, with a serious ChatGPT account-takeover flaw and a small setup improvement for Datasette.

bullets.text: Researchers chained several flaws in ChatGPT's HTML previews to hijack signed-in accounts via a shared link.
OpenAI fixed the hole and paid a $5,000 bug bounty, which Simon Willison considers low for such a serious flaw.
Datasette-llm 0.1a9 now uses the default model already set in LLM, so users can skip naming a model by hand.
